chapter_theme: Under the heading கீழ்மக்கள் செய்கை, seventeen verses on the conduct of base men: their insolence to the great, their denial of the next world, the danger of helping, reforming, provoking or living with them, their self-betraying speech and backbiting past shame, their deafness to counsel, their hidden ill will and whims, and the inverted world in which they rise.

107.reading: Petty men who neither perceive by the right way nor have any good nature, thinking the great easy to approach, set them level with themselves and speak unfitting words, and the verse calls this a dog barking at the moon.
107.nuance: The proverb works in two directions: the barking is the base man's insolence, and the moon, untouched and out of reach, is the great man's standing, so the insult is shown to be both noisy and harmless. எளியர் is what the petty think of the great, not what the great are.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is like a dog barking at the moon

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the petty man who speaks slightingly of the great as his equals

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the petty man's slighting of the great is empty noise that does not reach them

108.reading: Those who say 'is there any next world? get for yourselves all that the mind desires' are, the verse says, like people who have the cake of jaggery soaked in fragrant ghee thrown away and then, eyes streaming, feed on brick.
108.nuance: The image turns the materialist's offer upside down: he promises the fill of every desire, and the proverb says that what he really hands over is brick in place of a sweet, eaten in tears. The quotation marks open at கண்சொரீஇ, though the thrown-away ghee cake (lines 2-3) belongs to the same image. Whose eyes stream, the speaker's followers' or the speakers' own, the words leave open.

pazhamozhi.literal: those who, eyes streaming, feed (someone) brick

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to those who deny the next world and urge the fill of present desire

pazhamozhi.applied_to: denying the next world for present desire gives up a real good for a hard and painful one

109.reading: Those who, having read the mind of graceless base men, go close to them and do them good things without reckoning that trouble will come of it are, the verse says, plucking a tick from a tiger's face.
109.nuance: The good deed is real and the tick a real relief to the tiger, which is the point: the danger lies in the nature of the one helped, not in the help. கண்ணில names the lack of kindly regard (கண்ணோட்டம்) that makes them repay with harm.

pazhamozhi.literal: plucking off the tick on a tiger's face

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to anyone who does favours for the graceless base

pazhamozhi.applied_to: kindness done to the graceless base puts the doer within reach of their harm

110.reading: The verse tells the listener to correct his eagerness, asking whether the wicked ever come under control just because they have suffered, for even when chopped straw is worked into it unfit clay will not become a wall.
110.nuance: The straw stands for the hardship or correction mixed into the base man's life; the clay, not the binder, decides whether a wall stands. ஆர்வம் is the hope of reforming them, and the opening imperative turns the verse on the would-be reformer rather than the wicked.

pazhamozhi.literal: clay that does not bind will not make a wall

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the hope that suffering will reform the wicked

pazhamozhi.applied_to: hardship does not make the wicked tractable, because the fault is in their nature

111.reading: Men small by lineage, going in to settle a quarrel, rise up even against those who would part the fighters, and the verse likens this to white flour that, beaten to settle it firm on the ground, turns over and spills.
111.nuance: குலத்துச் சிறியார் is a birth term: it ranks people by the family they come from and lays the quarrelsome temper on that birth, though it could also mean those who are the mean ones of a family. The proverb is obscure; வெண்மா may be white flour or a pale animal, and காதி விடல் is taken here as spilling. The sense that the attempt to calm only overturns things is fairly secure; the image's detail is not.

norm.note: a birth-rank view of the period: quarrelsomeness is attributed to those of small lineage

pazhamozhi.literal: the white flour turning upside down and spilling

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the low-born peacemaker who turns on the peacemakers

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the base sent to calm a quarrel only overturn it further

112.reading: To keep in one's house, and to anger greatly, those who contradict what they are told, will not live in obedience, and take up a quarrel like a thrown stone is, the verse says, to pull out the axle-pin oneself while sitting inside the cart.
112.nuance: இல்இருந்து and உள்ளிருந்து answer each other: the defiant are inside the house as the rider is inside the cart, so the ruin is self-made and falls on the one who provokes them. The verse does not forbid keeping such men; it is the provoking (முனிவித்தல்) of them at close quarters that the proverb condemns.
112.domain_note: the head of a house and its unruly dependants

pazhamozhi.literal: like pulling out the axle-pin oneself from inside

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to one who provokes the defiant within his own house

pazhamozhi.applied_to: provoking the quarrelsome among one's own household undoes oneself

113.reading: To look after senseless people who know no shame, feel for no one, do worthless things and cherish nothing, to guide them and live together with them is, the verse says, like putting worms into a wound and binding it up.
113.nuance: The image makes the harm one's own care: the bandage that should heal the wound seals in what eats it. பேணி and ஒழுக்கி say the companion is not only tolerated but fostered.

pazhamozhi.literal: like putting in worms and binding up a wound

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to one who shelters and lives with the shameless

pazhamozhi.applied_to: fostering and living with the shameless lets the harm grow under one's own care

114.reading: The fool who speaks evil words and goes about hiding brings sorrow on himself by his own speech, the verse tells a good lady, as even the frog sunk and hidden in the sand perishes by its own mouth.
114.nuance: The frog's croak betrays its hiding place, so the proverb joins the two things the verse says of the fool: he hides, and he speaks, and the second undoes the first. The address நல்லாய்! is a frame.

pazhamozhi.literal: even a frog perishes by its own mouth

story.act: no story; the frog in the sand, betrayed by its croak, stands for the hidden man betrayed by his words

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the fool's own speech undoes the concealment he relies on

115.reading: Why blame those who speak well like kin when they meet a man and slander him behind his back when he has gone, having no eye for anything higher, since in any case for one whose nose is already cut off there is no further disgrace.
115.nuance: The verse does not excuse the backbiter; it says blame cannot touch him, because a man already disfigured has nothing left to lose by reproach. புறனழீஇ is the Kural's own word for backbiting (182).

pazhamozhi.literal: for one who has lost his nose there is no disgrace

story.act: no story; the noseless man, past disfigurement, is applied to the backbiter past shame

pazhamozhi.applied_to: reproach is wasted on the backbiter, who is already beyond shame

116.reading: It is hard to restrain with the tongue the qualityless brutes who speak unstrung words, lord of the shore where ships sway like drunkards, for no one catches the wind and puts it into a leather bag.
116.nuance: மாக்கள், not மக்கள், puts such men among beasts. The proverb gives the reason talk cannot curb them: their words are wind, which has no body to be held. The swaying ships of the address echo the unsteady talkers.

pazhamozhi.literal: no one catches the wind and puts it in a skin bag

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the attempt to silence loose talkers with words

pazhamozhi.applied_to: speech cannot restrain those whose speech has no substance

117.reading: Those who do not mind that the ignorant speak and that incapacity is bad, who do useless things, will not take the words of the great and do not guard themselves, are, the verse says, the ones who make others into thieves.
117.nuance: The proverb shifts the blame for a theft onto the careless owner: the man who leaves himself unguarded has made the thief. Line 1 is loosely joined; தெரியாதார் சொல்லும் திறனின்மை may be the ignorant man's talk and his want of skill taken together.

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to one who will not heed the great or guard himself

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the man who will not take counsel and guard himself invites the harm others do him

118.reading: One who has done a cruelty and will not speak so that its consequence may come to him sits wasting in distress, and the verse closes that for those who fear the public hall there is no remedy at all.
118.nuance: The proverb seems to say that the wrongdoer who will not face the assembly (மன்று) where wrongs are judged cuts himself off from the only remedy; dread of being judged keeps the cruelty unhealed. மரிசாதி is obscure, and the reading of lines 1-3 is tentative.

pazhamozhi.literal: for those who fear the assembly there is no remedy whatever

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the wrongdoer who will not bring his deed before the hall

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the wrongdoer who shuns judgement has no way to make amends

119.reading: The wicked conduct of the common run of people, who unlike the elders deserve scorn, is, lord of the good land where streams fall from the hill, like madness settled in the village hall.
119.nuance: The village hall (மன்றம்) is the most public place there is, so the proverb seems to say the base man's misconduct is open, settled and seen by all, not hidden. மன்னும் may mean 'lasting' or be an expletive; the contrast with முதுமக்கள் is not developed.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is like madness settled in the common hall

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the misconduct of common, scornworthy people

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the misconduct of the base is a standing public disorder

120.reading: Those who behave arrogantly and do unfitting things, who do uncaring things after being highly esteemed, and who vex others with a concealing heart are, the verse says, the gravel caught in a sandal.
120.nuance: The gravel is small, inside what one wears and walks on, and hurts at every step; the image fits men who are close, honoured and hidden in their hearts, not open enemies. பெருக்க மதித்தபின் makes the injury follow on the honour done them.

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to arrogant, ungrateful and concealing men kept close

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the hidden ill will of those one has honoured galls at every step

121.reading: To set someone up as one's close man and then remove him without any gain to him is a deed fitted to smallness, and the verse likens it to little children planting a grove.
121.nuance: Children plant twigs in play and pull them up the same day, so the proverb names the fault as whim: installing and removing without reason. பெறுமாற்றம் இன்றி can mean without his gaining anything or without any cause found in him.

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to one who raises a man to intimacy and drops him without cause

pazhamozhi.applied_to: casting off without cause one raised to intimacy is childish smallness

122.reading: When the worthy, full in speech, live withdrawn and those without self-restraint stand tall and flourish, lord of the hill where bright falls come down, that is the gourd sinking and the grinding stone floating.
122.nuance: The proverb is an impossibility, so the verse calls the state of things against nature, not merely unjust. The measure of rank is conduct and speech (உரைசான்ற, நிறையுளர் அல்லார்), not birth or wealth.

pazhamozhi.literal: the gourd sinking and the grinding stone floating

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to a time when the worthy sink and the unrestrained rise

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the rise of the unworthy over the worthy is an inversion of nature

123.reading: Those who, without discernment or kindly regard and without fear of evil deeds, speak slightingly to all who come to them and do what all the skilled and accomplished hate are answered by the question whether there is no poison for the people of hell.
123.nuance: The proverb makes such men hell's own people; whether it means that poison is their due or that they are the poison hell holds, the words do not settle. தீர்ந்த விரகர் are those finished in skill.

pazhamozhi.literal: is there no poison for the dwellers in hell?

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to graceless men who fear no evil and slight everyone

pazhamozhi.applied_to: men without grace or fear of evil are already of hell and merit its poison

links.note: Naladiyar 70 tells the high not to answer the low, as no one bites back a biting dog; Pazhamozhi 107 sets the base man's slighting talk as a dog barking at the moon.
links.teaches: Read together the dog moves from biting to barking out of reach: the Naladiyar asks the great to refrain from answering, and Pazhamozhi shows the insult never reaches them anyway.
links.list_adds: its proverb puts the insulted great man out of the dog's range, so restraint is backed by the insult's harmlessness, which the quatrain does not claim.

links.note: 107 has the base set the great level with themselves in speech; 122 has the unrestrained rise while the worthy withdraw.
links.teaches: The two verses give the same inversion at two scales, one man's insolent equal talk and a whole order where stone floats, and show the first as the seed of the second.

links.note: Naladiyar 329 says the small-minded think of the next world only in want and illness; Pazhamozhi 108 gives the base man who denies it outright and urges the fill of desire.
links.teaches: The pair sets two degrees of the same neglect, forgetting the next world when able and denying it as a creed, and Pazhamozhi's proverb names the cost the Naladiyar leaves implied, brick eaten in tears.
links.list_adds: it quotes the denier's own words and answers them with an image of the trade he offers, where the quatrain only describes the forgetter's timing.

links.note: Kural 850 says one who says 'it is not' to what the world says is will be reckoned a demon; Pazhamozhi 108 names one such denial, of the next world, and its practical upshot.
links.teaches: The couplet leaves blank what is denied; the pairing fills it with the next world and shows the denier's error as a bad exchange, not only a social stigma.
links.list_adds: it fills the couplet's blank with a named denial and a proverb that judges it by what is lost, not by the world's verdict.

links.note: Sirupanchamoolam 16 says that before the worthless anger is good and nobility bad, as good meat is wasted in a biting dog's mouth; Pazhamozhi 109 says good done to the graceless base puts the doer in danger.
links.teaches: Holding them together shows the two halves of one counsel: Sirupanchamoolam says kindness to the base is wasted, Pazhamozhi that it is also dangerous, the tiger's face being closer than the dog's mouth.

links.note: Kural 1078 says the base yield their use only when crushed like sugar-cane; Pazhamozhi 110 asks whether the wicked ever come under control because they have suffered and answers no. The conflict holds on the reading that the Kural's crushing and Pazhamozhi's suffering are both pressure applied to the base.
links.teaches: The pair splits on whether pressure works on the base: the Kural finds something sweet to be pressed out, Pazhamozhi finds clay that no binder will make into a wall.
links.list_adds: its proverb puts the fault in the material itself, so that no admixture of hardship helps, against the couplet's cane that yields under force.

links.note: Nanmanikkadigai 98 says the base, though bound and scoured, show their dirt; Pazhamozhi 110 says suffering does not tame the wicked, as unfit clay makes no wall.
links.teaches: Both deny that working on the base changes them, and together they cover the two methods of correction, scouring from outside and mixing in from within, each failing on the material.

links.note: Kural 972 says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from deeds; Pazhamozhi 111 lays the quarrelsome temper on those small by lineage. The conflict holds on the reading that குலத்துச் சிறியார் ranks by birth rather than naming the mean ones of a family.
links.teaches: Set beside the Kural, the verse shows the ethics books divided on whether baseness is inherited: the couplet ranks by deeds, Pazhamozhi traces a vice to the family one comes from.
links.list_adds: it attaches a specific behaviour, turning on peacemakers, to a birth group, the very link between birth and worth the couplet denies.

links.note: Naladiyar 68 says the anger of the low keeps spreading and never dies; Pazhamozhi 111 shows it spreading onto those who come to part the fighters.
links.teaches: Pazhamozhi gives the Naladiyar's spreading anger its concrete path, from the quarrel to the peacemakers themselves, so that intervention becomes one of the ways it spreads.
links.list_adds: its proverb shows the attempt to settle the quarrel as what overturns it, a turn the quatrain's general claim lacks.

links.note: Kural 888 says a family with inner enmity wears itself down like gold rubbing a file; Pazhamozhi 112 says provoking the defiant within one's own house is pulling the axle-pin from inside the cart.
links.teaches: Together they show inner enmity as both a slow wearing and a sudden collapse, and Pazhamozhi places its cause with the householder who provokes it, not with the enmity alone.
links.list_adds: its proverb makes the head of the house the agent of the ruin, sitting inside what he dismantles, where the couplet speaks of the family as a whole.

links.note: Kural 451 says greatness fears small company while smallness takes it at once as kin; Pazhamozhi 113 says fostering and living with the shameless is binding worms into a wound.
links.teaches: The couplet explains why the great fear such company, and the pairing supplies what they fear: harm that grows under one's own care, sealed in by the very bandage of fellowship.
links.list_adds: its proverb makes one's care for the base the means of one's injury, a mechanism the couplet's fear leaves unstated.

links.note: 109 warns against doing good to the graceless base; 113 against fostering and living with the shameless.
links.teaches: Read in order the two verses rise from a single favour to a shared life, and the danger rises with them from a tiger's sudden bite to a wound eaten from within.

links.note: Kural 127 says those who do not guard the tongue suffer from the fault of their words; Pazhamozhi 114 shows the hiding fool betrayed by his own evil speech, like the frog in the sand.
links.teaches: Pazhamozhi adds what the Kural does not consider, that the unguarded tongue undoes even a man who has hidden himself, so concealment is no substitute for restraint of speech.
links.list_adds: its proverb sets hiding against speaking and lets speech win, a contrast the couplet's single command lacks.

links.note: Kural 182 ranks backbiting with a false smile as worse than open wrongdoing; Pazhamozhi 115 asks why blame the backbiter at all, since he is past disgrace.
links.teaches: The Kural's ranking condemns the backbiter most severely, and Pazhamozhi warns that this condemnation does him no harm, since a man without shame is beyond the reach of blame.
links.list_adds: its proverb turns from judging the backbiter to judging the use of blaming him, adding a limit of blame the couplet does not raise.

links.note: Nanmanikkadigai 10 says the base are bound with iron after goading while the worthy are bound by courtesy; Pazhamozhi 116 says the qualityless cannot be restrained by words.
links.teaches: Together they mark a limit of persuasion: courtesy binds the worthy, but words are wind to the base, so only force is left, as the Nanmanikkadigai says outright.

links.note: Naladiyar 70 says the high do not answer the low with their own mouths; Pazhamozhi 116 says it is hard to restrain loose talkers by speech at all.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar's refusal to answer the base is a matter of dignity, and Pazhamozhi adds a practical ground: answering is useless, since words cannot catch wind.
links.list_adds: its proverb gives a reason of futility beside the quatrain's reason of rank.

links.note: Kural 448 says a ruler without rebukers perishes even with no one to ruin him; Pazhamozhi 117 says one who will not take the words of the great and does not guard himself makes others into thieves.
links.teaches: The Kural's ruin needs no enemy; Pazhamozhi adds that the unguarded man's ruin creates its own agents, so the thief is partly his making.
links.list_adds: it carries the couplet's claim from the king to anyone and its proverb shifts guilt from the thief to the man who would not heed counsel.

links.note: Kural 821 calls the friendship of those close without inner consent an anvil for striking when the chance comes; Pazhamozhi 120 calls the arrogant, concealing men one has honoured gravel in a sandal.
links.teaches: The two images of hidden ill will differ in timing: the Kural's waits for its moment to strike, Pazhamozhi's galls at every step, so the false intimate is shown as both a threat and a constant wearing.
links.list_adds: its proverb turns hidden hostility into a present, continuous injury, where the couplet looks to a single future blow.

links.note: Kural 510 says that doubting one already trusted brings endless trouble; Pazhamozhi 121 says raising a man to intimacy and casting him off without cause is a deed of smallness.
links.teaches: The Kural counts the cost of withdrawing trust to the one who withdraws; Pazhamozhi judges the character of the act, a child's play with a grove, so the error is both costly and mean.
links.list_adds: its proverb names the fault as whim and smallness, a moral judgement beside the couplet's prudential one.

links.note: Naladiyar 368 says the old wealthy and the worthy decline while concubines' sons and the base flourish, the world upside down; Pazhamozhi 122 says the worthy withdraw while the unrestrained rise, the gourd sinking and the stone floating.
links.teaches: Both read social inversion through an image, but the Naladiyar mixes birth and wealth into its ranks while Pazhamozhi measures only by speech and restraint, showing the complaint can be made on conduct alone.
links.list_adds: it drops the quatrain's birth and wealth markers and ranks by conduct, and its proverb calls the inversion impossible in nature, not merely a turned umbrella.

links.note: Naladiyar 348 lists the base as harsh, without kindly regard and scornful of all; Pazhamozhi 123 names the same traits and adds the absence of fear of evil deeds and a verdict of hell.
links.teaches: The quatrain describes and stops; Pazhamozhi takes nearly the same portrait and passes sentence, so the pairing shows the description turning into a judgement.
links.list_adds: its proverb closes the portrait with a verdict, making such men hell's own, where the quatrain gives only the list.

source_issues: 108 lines 2-4: the quotation opens at கண்சொரீஇ, leaving the thrown-away ghee cake of lines 2-3 outside though it is part of the proverb's image; the quotation marks may be misplaced.
111 line 3-4: வெண்மாத் தலைக்கீழாக் காதி விடல் is obscure (வெண்மா, காதி).
112 line 2: கல்எறிந்தாற் போலத் கலாந்தலை has an unexpected த் after போல; probably a typing slip for போலக்.
118 line 3: மரிசாதி is obscure, and the quotation opens mid-line at மன்றஞ்சு.
